title: KV cache deferred writeback topology and retention safety
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a deferred writeback topology for the KV cache aimed at reducing peak write amplification, improving eviction safety under fragmentation, and enabling predictable memory retention across multi-tenant workloads. The design separates admission and eviction control from physical writeback to disk/spill/host memory and introduces a staged writeback pipeline with retention safety checks to prevent accidental eviction regressions during heavy churn.

Goals:
- Ensure that eviction decisions do not immediately trigger expensive writeback operations that amplify memory pressure or increase latencies for tail requests.
- Maintain safe retention semantics so that a tenant cannot lose KV state due to transient spikes or background compaction.
- Reduce fragmentation amplification by grouping writebacks and scheduling them against low-utilization stripes/lanes.
- Expose observable signals (per-tenant retention pressure, deferred writeback backlog, fragmentation ratio) for automated policy tuning.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full rewrite of the allocator. It builds on the existing lane/stripe abstractions and memory pools. It does not change the on-disk format for spill files.

Background and motivation:
Current behavior observed in stress tests: eviction triggers synchronous writeback for dirty KV entries. Under sustained churn (many short-lived prefixes), the system sees a cascade: eviction -> immediate writeback -> spike in IO and CPU for serialization -> temporary increase in memory use (buffers) -> more evictions. This feedback loop causes higher fragmentation and sometimes out-of-memory (OOM) on host-level Dedicated nodes.

We observed three patterns that motivate deferred writeback:
1) Hot churn: short sequences of insert/delete where writeback is unnecessary if an item is re-admitted soon after eviction.
2) IO contention: simultaneous writebacks across shards increase tail latency for inference serving.
3) Fragmentation windows: immediate compaction attempts after an eviction can conflict with allocator heuristics and produce suboptimal packing.

Design overview (staged pipeline):
1) Admission/eviction decision layer (unchanged): the admission controller still marks slots as candidate-for-eviction or retained.
2) Deferred writeback queue (DWQ): items evicted-from-active caches are appended to a per-shard, per-tenant DWQ instead of being synchronously written. Each DWQ entry includes metadata: key, tenant, hint (priority), sequence version, and a retention deadline.
3) Retention safety check: before a DWQ entry is flushed, the system re-checks if the key was re-populated (version mismatch) or if the retention policy for this tenant has changed (e.g., temporary no-evict window for debugging). If re-populated, writeback is dropped.
4) Batched writeback workers: background workers consume DWQs and writeback in topology-aware batches. Workers pick DWQ entries according to stripe affinity and current IO/CPU load.
5) Completion and reconciler: upon persistence, metadata is updated; if persistence fails after retry budget, the system can either escalate (mark tenant-critical) or re-enqueue with backoff.

Topology and lanes: stripe-aware retention lanes
- Each shard exposes N writeback lanes. Lanes are grouped by stripe affinity (stripe == logical region intended to reduce cross-NUMA traffic).
- Lanes are prioritized by a composite score: tenant_sla_priority * (1 + retention_pressure) * (1 - fragmentation_hotness).
- A small fraction of lanes are reserved for low-latency or high-SLA tenants so that background drains do not interfere with critical writebacks.

Memory pools and buffers:
- DWQ entries are lightweight descriptors stored in a ring buffer per-lane to avoid heap churn. Payloads are not copied until a worker starts the writeback and pins the source slot.
- A single shared writeback buffer pool (configurable size) is used for serialization to reduce per-writeback allocations; workers borrow buffers and return them. Buffer size tuned to expected average entry size for embeddings metadata + prefix.
- Borrow/return policy: if the pool is exhausted, low-priority lanes stall (backpressure to DWQ admission) rather than allocate. This avoids uncontrolled memory growth under writeback storms.

Retention safety primitives:
- Sequence versioning: every KV item carries a monotonic insert/update sequence. DWQ records the sequence at eviction time; before writeback, the sequence in cache is re-read—if mismatch, drop writeback.
- Soft retention deadlines: configurable per-tenant TTL (not the same as item TTL) that prevents eviction writeback for a short window post-eviction (e.g., 5s for bursty workloads). This allows quick re-admissions to avoid redundant writes.
- Forced flush API: ops team can call an emergency flush for a tenant (bypasses soft deadlines) in maintenance windows.

Fragmentation mitigation strategies:
- Grouped draining: the batched writer attempts to pack writebacks into stripe-local contiguous ranges to allow allocator-friendly free runs; the completion reconciler can then trigger compaction more efficiently on coalesced segments.
- Adaptive coalescing threshold: if fragmentation ratio > X% and background IO is low, writer increases coalescing window size to compress many small writebacks into a single larger writeback operation.
- Compact-on-low-memory: when free memory within a stripe falls under threshold, a prioritized compaction pass is scheduled after draining select lanes.

Failure modes and backpressure:
- DWQ growth: bounding ring sizes per-tenant prevents a noisy tenant from filling global queues. When bound is hit, admission controller switches to immediate eviction + drop-writeback (best-effort) for lowest-priority tenants and emits alerts.
- Persistent writeback failures: after N retries, entries are moved to a tombstone queue and the tenant/team is paged if the entries are marked critical per SLA.
- IO starvation for serving: workers dynamically reduce concurrency when latency SLOs for serving threads degrade (observed via p99 latency signal). This is achieved by an admission token bucket that both serving and writeback workers draw from; priority lending favors serving paths.

Observability and metrics (required):
- dwq_length_per_shard_lane{shard, lane, tenant} gauge
- dwq_enqueue_rate and dwq_dequeue_rate counters
- deferred_writeback_success_rate, retry_count, failure_count
- retention_drop_count (number of writebacks dropped due to re-population)
- fragmentation_ratio_per_stripe gauge
- writeback_batch_size histogram
- reserved_lane_blocked_time for SLA lanes
- alerts: dwq_exceeded_per_tenant (warn), persistent_writeback_fail (critical), writeback_vs_serve_latency_sla_cross (critical)

Experiments and rollout plan:
Phase 0 - simulation (2 weeks):
- Run micro-simulator using historical traces (from kafka:kv-cache-events-{prod,hst}) to calibrate DWQ ring sizes, soft deadline defaults, and coalescing thresholds.
- Goal: find parameters that reduce write-amplification by >=20% in churny traces while keeping dropped writebacks <1% for high-SLA tenants.

Phase 1 - guarded beta (4 weeks):
- Feature flag per-cluster, per-shard. Start with non-prod clusters. Enable reserve lanes at 10%, soft deadline 3s, ring size 8k entries.
- Instrument extensive metrics and synthetic load tests.

Phase 2 - limited prod (4–6 weeks):
- Enable on a small subset of Dedicated pools, low-risk tenants. Monitor p99 serving latency, retention_drop_count, and fragmentation_ratio.

Phase 3 - global rollout and autotune (ongoing):
- Enable autopolicy that adjusts soft_deadline and lane reservations based on observed retention_drop_count and slab fragmentation.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- Soft deadline tuning: short deadlines reduce risk of lost durability guarantees but increase writeback rate; long deadlines save IO but risk leaving dirty state non-persisted longer. We need an SRE/SEC/LEGAL check for acceptable windows for enterprise customers.
- Consistency model: dropping a writeback because the key was re-populated is safe for many uses, but we must ensure we do not break cross-tenant snapshots or audit requirements.
- Spill format efficiency: grouping writebacks introduces larger records in spill files. We should validate spill ingestion performance when records become larger/coalesced.

Action items:
- Marcus: implement DWQ ring prototype (P0) and a simple worker loop—due 2024-11-20. Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/443
- Priya: simulate traces and produce a parameter sweep report for soft_deadline and ring size—due 2024-11-26.
- Ethan: add observability scaffolding to the metric pipeline and dashboards for dwq metrics—due 2024-12-02.
- Ava (owner): coordinate SRE/Legal review of soft-deadline safe windows and finalize rollout gating checklist—due 2024-12-09.

References and related docs:
- Confluence: KV Cache perf benchmarks and trace corpus (linked_artifacts above)
- Existing allocator notes: see cache-slot-coalescer and slab-rehoming playbooks for compaction interaction
- Slack threads: #infra-kv-cache recent incident log (2024-10-18)

Notes to reviewers (early feedback wanted):
- Are the DWQ ring sizes and the backpressure semantics reasonable for multi-tenant isolation?
- Any compliance/retention concerns with dropping writebacks during re-population?
- Suggestions for additional observability or safe-fail behaviors we should include in the first beta.

This draft is intentionally pragmatic: we lean on per-shard lightweight metadata and background batched writeback rather than forcing synchronous IO on the eviction path. If accepted, the next step will be a behaviorally compatible prototype that can be toggled at runtime.
